howToMeasure.text: Rest quietly for at least 5 minutes before checking. Place your index and middle fingers on the inside of your wrist below the thumb, and count the beats for 60 seconds while seated.
howToMeasure.source: American Heart Association: All About Heart Rate (Pulse)

whyItMatters.text: A typical resting heart rate for adults ranges from 60 to 100 beats per minute. Highly trained athletes may have a resting heart rate as low as 40 beats per minute.
whyItMatters.source: American Heart Association: All About Heart Rate (Pulse)

hazardEffects.text: In microgravity, cephalad fluid shifts and plasma volume loss alter autonomic cardiovascular regulation, which can impact orthostatic tolerance during gravity transitions.
hazardEffects.source: NASA Human Research Roadmap: Risk of Orthostatic Intolerance

selfCare.text: Rest seated quietly for 5 to 10 minutes and repeat the measurement to verify the reading.
Verify fluid intake and consider electrolyte replacement following countermeasure exercise sessions.

whenToEscalate.text: Notify the Crew Medical Officer if resting heart rate is consistently above 100 bpm, drops below 40 bpm (or below known athletic baseline), or occurs alongside chest pain, shortness of breath, or dizziness.

howToMeasure.text: Position the forehead Double Sensor heat-flux device securely against the skin during pre-exercise rest. Avoid taking measurements immediately after intense physical activity.

whyItMatters.text: Body temperature measures the body's ability to generate and dissipate heat. Typical resting temperature in adults averages around 37°C (98.6°F) and fluctuates across the daily cycle.

hazardEffects.text: Resting core body temperature in astronauts gradually increases by approximately 1°C over the first 75 mission days in microgravity; authors note a possible correlation with impaired convective heat dissipation and systemic inflammatory markers rather than established causation.

selfCare.text: Rest in an area with active cabin ventilation and airflow to promote convective cooling.
Drink water and repeat the temperature measurement after 20 to 30 minutes of inactive rest.

whenToEscalate.text: Notify the Crew Medical Officer if core temperature exceeds 38.5°C (101.3°F), does not return toward baseline after resting, or is accompanied by chills or acute malaise.

howToMeasure.text: Rest seated quietly for 5 minutes with feet flat and arm supported at heart level before taking a brachial cuff measurement. Avoid talking during cuff inflation.
howToMeasure.source: American Heart Association: Understanding Blood Pressure Readings

whyItMatters.text: Blood pressure reflects systemic vascular resistance and arterial load. A typical resting terrestrial reading is systolic below 120 mmHg and diastolic below 80 mmHg.
whyItMatters.source: American Heart Association: Understanding Blood Pressure Readings

hazardEffects.text: Long-duration microgravity induces cephalad fluid redistribution and arterial remodeling, resulting in an average drop of ~8 mmHg systolic and ~9 mmHg diastolic over 24-hour ambulatory monitoring.
hazardEffects.source: Norsk et al. 2015, Journal of Physiology

selfCare.text: If a spot measurement is unusually high or low, remain quietly seated for 5 minutes and repeat the measurement on the same arm.
Stay mindful of hydration status, as plasma volume depletion directly exacerbates orthostatic blood pressure drops.
selfCare.source: NASA Human Research Roadmap: Risk of Orthostatic Intolerance

whenToEscalate.text: Notify the Crew Medical Officer immediately if systolic exceeds 180 mmHg, diastolic exceeds 120 mmHg, or if blood pressure deviation is accompanied by vision changes, acute headache, or chest pain.
whenToEscalate.source: American Heart Association: Understanding Blood Pressure Readings (Hypertensive Crisis)

howToMeasure.text: Clean the puncture site, dry thoroughly, and apply a fresh capillary blood sample to an approved glucometer test strip, noting whether the test is fasting or post-meal.
howToMeasure.source: NIDDK: Continuous Glucose Monitoring and Blood Glucose Testing

whyItMatters.text: Blood glucose reflects metabolic carbohydrate regulation. In fasting adults, typical levels sit between 70 and 99 mg/dL, rising below 140 mg/dL two hours post-meal.

hazardEffects.text: Physical inactivity in confined habitats combined with spaceflight-induced insulin resistance can alter glucose tolerance and postprandial glycemic clearance.
hazardEffects.source: NASA Human Research Program: Risk of Adverse Health Outcomes from Altered Nutrition

selfCare.text: If a fasting reading is unexpectedly low, consume 15 grams of fast-acting carbohydrates (e.g., fruit pouch) and re-check in 15 minutes.
Log nutritional intake and schedule physical countermeasure exercise to assist insulin sensitivity.

whenToEscalate.text: Notify the Crew Medical Officer if blood glucose drops below 54 mg/dL (severe hypoglycemia) or exceeds 250 mg/dL with associated nausea, weakness, or mental confusion.

howToMeasure.text: Log total sleep duration over the preceding 24-hour crew duty cycle, including any planned or unplanned restorative naps.

whyItMatters.text: Adequate sleep is critical for neurobehavioral performance, vigilance, and immune function. Adults typically require 7 or more hours per night.

hazardEffects.text: Circadian rhythm disruption, lack of natural sunlight cycles, operational noise, and sleep cabin microgravity discomfort frequently cause fragmented sleep and cumulative sleep debt.
hazardEffects.source: NASA Human Research Program: Risk of Performance Decrements from Sleep Loss

selfCare.text: Optimize personal sleep station environment: verify earplugs are secured, use sleep mask to block ambient light, and ensure cabin ventilation fan is unobstructed.
Review sleep hygiene: minimize bright screen and high-intensity blue light exposure within 60 minutes of scheduled sleep.

whenToEscalate.text: Notify the Crew Medical Officer if cumulative sleep drops below 4 hours for consecutive duty cycles or if daytime drowsiness impairs critical operational mission tasks.

howToMeasure.text: Select an integer rating from 1 (very low) to 5 (very good) reflecting subjective emotional state and operational stress over the last 24 hours.

whyItMatters.text: Self-reported mood tracks cognitive resilience, psychological adaptation, and interpersonal crew dynamics during isolated, confined, and extreme mission phases.

hazardEffects.text: Prolonged confinement in small quarters, extreme distance from family, and heavy mission workloads can contribute to asthenia, sensory monotony, and interpersonal tension.
hazardEffects.source: NASA Human Research Program: Risk of Adverse Behavioral Conditions and Psychiatric Disorders

selfCare.text: Engage in planned recreational time, private communications with ground support networks, or personal audio/visual decompression activities.
Discuss workload adjustments with crewmates if cognitive fatigue is compounding.

whenToEscalate.text: Reach out to the Crew Medical Officer or operational psychologist if sustained low mood, anxiety, or apathy begins impacting daily mission tasks.
